strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: uncertainty quantification for machine-learned interatomic potentials, especially in low-data and out-of-distribution regimes where ensembles are expensive.

The proposed BLIP framework is practically motivated and potentially useful: an adaptive variational-dropout wrapper for message-passing MLIPs that can be used for training from scratch and for fine-tuning pretrained potentials.

Empirical results are promising across several settings. BLIP improves over MC dropout on the charged-particle task, improves force MAE and ECE on the ammonia OOD benchmark, and appears to improve ORB v3 fine-tuning on silica glass while giving calibrated force uncertainties.
The manuscript is mostly clear and includes useful implementation details in the appendix, including datasets, metrics, training hyperparameters, and pseudocode.

The paper is honest about an important architectural limitation: the current equivariance argument applies only to certain learnable layers and excludes important equivariant MLIPs such as MACE and UMA.
weaknesses: The Bayesian formulation is not fully convincing. The variational posterior is input-conditioned and the stated prior variance depends on the learned weights theta, which makes the interpretation as standard variational Bayesian inference unclear. The KL derivation appears simplified and does not discuss these conceptual issues or their consequences.

Several central claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly claims architecture-agnostic integration and minimal or no additional inference cost, but the method is not compatible with major equivariant architectures in its current form, and uncertainty estimation still requires many stochastic forward passes. The MAP-only inference has deterministic cost but does not provide uncertainty.

The empirical evaluation is promising but not yet sufficiently robust for the breadth of the claims. The main MLIP experiments cover only ammonia and silica, with no molecular dynamics stability tests, active-learning loop, or evaluation on broader chemistry/materials benchmarks where UQ quality would matter operationally.

Comparisons to baselines are incomplete. Some baseline results are taken from prior work without uncertainty over seeds, Deep Ensemble entries have missing standard deviations, and the silica results are shown mainly in a figure without detailed numerical tables for all metrics and training sizes. It is difficult to assess statistical significance and fairness.

The claimed calibration evidence is limited. ECE and Spearman correlation are useful, but the paper lacks reliability diagrams, NLL/CRPS for the MLIP tasks, sensitivity to number of MC samples, and analysis of whether uncertainty remains reliable under stronger distribution shifts.

Reproducibility is only partial. The manuscript says code is available but the URL is blank in the extracted text, and several method choices appear tuned per setting, including KL weights, prior dropout probabilities, and clamp ranges. These hyperparameters may strongly affect performance and calibration, but no ablation or sensitivity study is provided.

Originality is moderate rather than high. Adaptive variational dropout and local reparameterization are established; the contribution is mainly adapting them to MLIPs. That adaptation is useful, but the paper should more clearly separate what is new from inherited Bayesian dropout machinery.

Presentation has some issues: there are typos such as “data-scarse” and “computional,” some notation is inconsistent, and the method section sometimes describes weights as stochastic per input in a way that blurs the distinction between Bayesian weight uncertainty and heteroscedastic input-dependent noise.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: uncertainty quantification for machine-learning interatomic potentials, especially in low-data and out-of-distribution settings where deep ensembles are expensive.

The proposed adaptive variational-dropout formulation is plausibly useful as a relatively lightweight wrapper around some message-passing MLIP architectures, and the paper explains how symmetry preservation can hold when the inference network produces invariant dropout coefficients.

The experiments cover several regimes: a controlled N-body system, an OOD ammonia benchmark, and fine-tuning a pretrained ORB model on a larger silica system. This is a sensible empirical direction, and some reported numbers, especially force MAE and ECE on ammonia/silica, are promising.

The appendix gives dataset sources, broad training hyperparameters, and pseudocode, and the paper acknowledges an important architectural limitation: the current formulation does not directly cover major equivariant MLIPs such as MACE or UMA.
weaknesses: The central Bayesian framing is not technically convincing as written. The variational posterior is input-dependent, q(w|h0,aij), so it is closer to amortized stochastic regularization than a standard posterior over weights after observing the training set. The paper does not clearly justify this probabilistic model or explain what posterior is being approximated at test time.

The prior/KL construction appears problematic. The prior variance is defined using the trainable weights theta, and the KL derivation in the appendix is terse and seems to omit dimensional constants/factors. This undermines the claim of principled variational Bayesian inference, which is a central contribution.

The evaluation is too thin for the broad claims. There are only two true MLIP datasets, and the strongest empirical claims rely on a small ammonia benchmark and one silica fine-tuning setup. There is no active-learning experiment, no molecular-dynamics stability test, no coverage/reliability diagrams, and limited analysis of failure cases.

Baseline comparisons are not fully satisfying. Several ammonia baselines are copied from Tan et al. rather than rerun under matched implementations, uncertainty results for silica are only reported for the 1024-sample setting, and deep ensemble results often lack seed variation or standard errors. The N-body table even reports NA uncertainty for ensemble variation despite averaging claims elsewhere.

The efficiency claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly says BLIP has minimal or no additional inference cost, but uncertainty estimation uses many stochastic forward passes, and the low-cost MAP path does not provide uncertainty. No wall-clock, memory, parameter-count, or throughput measurements are provided to substantiate the computational-overhead claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript says code is available but leaves the URL blank. Important details are missing or unclear, including exact split files, all random seeds, number of MC samples for all experiments, exact baseline implementations, and full numeric silica results behind Figure 3.

Presentation has many issues that reduce confidence: typos such as 'data-scarse', 'memebers', and 'computional'; inconsistent notation; unclear table labels; and some claims that exceed the evidence. The impact/ethics statement is generic and does not discuss possible misuse or reliability risks of uncertain atomistic simulations.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: uncertainty quantification for machine-learning interatomic potentials in low-data and OOD settings, where deep ensembles are often too expensive.

The proposed BLIP framework is conceptually useful: it wraps message/update networks with adaptive variational dropout, supports training from scratch and fine-tuning, and is presented as largely architecture-agnostic within an explicit symmetry analysis.

Empirical results are encouraging across three settings. BLIP improves or matches strong baselines on N-body dynamics, ammonia OOD prediction, and ORB v3 fine-tuning on silica, with particularly strong force MAE and ECE results in the chemistry tasks.

The paper includes relevant uncertainty metrics beyond point error, including NLL/CRPS, ECE, and Spearman correlation between predicted variance and squared error, which are appropriate for the intended active-learning use case.
The appendix provides useful implementation detail, including dataset links, hyperparameters, posterior-network descriptions, and inference/training pseudocode.
weaknesses: The variational formulation is not fully convincing. The prior appears to depend on the learned deterministic weights, and the KL derivation is unusual and insufficiently justified; this weakens the claim of principled Bayesian inference.

The claimed architecture-agnostic nature is overstated. The authors acknowledge that the current method does not directly cover important equivariant MLIPs such as MACE and UMA, which are central architectures in the target domain.

The empirical comparison is promising but not yet definitive. Some baselines for ammonia and silica are taken from Tan et al. rather than rerun under the same model family and tuning budget, while the strongest ORB-based comparisons are limited mostly to deterministic fine-tuning and a 4-member ensemble.

Efficiency claims are under-supported. The paper repeatedly claims minimal overhead or deterministic-level inference cost, but does not provide wall-clock training/inference time, memory use, or MC-sample cost comparisons across BLIP, MC dropout, and ensembles.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the main text says code is available but the URL is missing. Although hyperparameters and datasets are described, reproducing the central ORB v3 fine-tuning experiments would still require code and exact split/configuration details.

The evaluation scope is somewhat narrow for a general MLIP UQ method: only one small molecular OOD dataset and one large silica fine-tuning dataset are used, with no active-learning loop or molecular-dynamics stability demonstration despite those being major motivating applications.

Presentation is generally clear, but there are several typos and imprecise statements, including “data-scarse,” “deepensembling,” and a loose explanation of ECE as classification-style confidence, which should be tightened for a camera-ready version.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: uncertainty quantification for ML interatomic potentials in data-scarce, OOD, and pretrained fine-tuning settings.

The method is practically attractive: a lightweight input-dependent variational dropout mechanism that can be inserted into message-passing MLIPs and used either for stochastic UQ or deterministic MAP-style prediction.
Empirical coverage is broader than many UQ papers in this area: N-body dynamics, NH3 OOD force/energy prediction, SiO2 fine-tuning, and MATPES active learning.

Results are promising: BLIP improves over MC dropout, often improves deterministic fine-tuning, and is competitive with or better than deep ensembles on several MAE, ECE, NLL, and CRPS metrics while using one backbone model.
The paper includes useful implementation details, dataset sources, hyperparameters, algorithms, and a computational-cost table, which supports partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The Bayesian formulation is not fully sound. The variational posterior is conditioned on each input structure, which makes the weights data-point-dependent; this is closer to stochastic hypernetwork/adaptive dropout than a standard posterior over global model weights. The paper nevertheless repeatedly claims principled variational Bayesian inference without adequately justifying this model.

The prior is unusual and problematic: it is zero-mean but has variance proportional to the trainable mean weights theta^2. This makes the prior depend on learned parameters, creates degeneracies near zero weights, and undermines the interpretation of the KL as a Bayesian regularizer.

There appear to be mathematical inconsistencies in the variance parameterization. Eq. 5 defines variance as alpha * theta^2, Eq. 7 samples epsilon with variance alpha, Algorithm 1 uses alpha as a standard-deviation multiplier, and the KL expression appears to omit standard Gaussian KL factors. These issues affect the central training objective, not just notation.

The main efficiency claim is somewhat overstated. Deterministic MAP inference has no UQ; uncertainty requires many stochastic forward passes, and the paper admits sampling has training-like FLOPs. Thus claims of uncertainty with minimal inference overhead need clearer qualification and wall-clock evidence.

Experimental comparisons are not fully convincing. Several baselines for NH3 and SiO2 are taken from Tan et al. rather than rerun under identical code/training budgets, while BLIP receives new tuning and pretrained ORB v3 in some settings. This complicates attribution of gains to the Bayesian method itself.

Deep ensembles remain better on some important metrics, e.g. EGNN N-body NLL/CRPS and SiO2 Spearman correlation, but the discussion tends to frame BLIP as broadly superior. Statistical testing is absent, and some reported improvements are small relative to variance or missing baseline variance.

The active-learning experiment is suggestive but limited: it uses labeled MATPES data as a DFT proxy, compares only random vs BLIP uncertainty selection, and does not compare against ensemble uncertainty or standard AL acquisition baselines, making the AL contribution hard to judge.

The architecture-agnostic claim is too strong. The paper itself notes limitations for important equivariant architectures such as MACE and UMA under the local reparameterization implementation, yet the abstract and conclusion present the method as generally architecture-agnostic.

Uncertainty evaluation is incomplete. ECE, NLL/CRPS, and Spearman are useful, but the paper does not deeply analyze calibration under distribution shift, failure cases, aleatoric vs epistemic uncertainty, or robustness to number of Monte Carlo samples and KL/dropout hyperparameters.

Reproducibility is moderate but incomplete: datasets and many hyperparameters are listed, but code, exact splits/checkpoints for pretrained fine-tuning, baseline rerun settings, and compute-time measurements are not provided in sufficient detail for reliable independent replication.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: uncertainty quantification for machine-learned interatomic potentials, especially in low-data, OOD, fine-tuning, and active learning regimes where uncertainty estimates are genuinely useful.

The proposed approach is simple to integrate conceptually: add input-dependent variational dropout/noise to message and update functions, with a lightweight inference network producing perturbation scales. This could be a useful engineering direction if made technically precise.

The manuscript evaluates on several relevant settings, including N-body dynamics, ammonia OOD prediction, silica glass fine-tuning, and MATPES active learning. The reported results often show improved predictive error and calibration relative to some baselines.

The appendix includes useful implementation details, dataset descriptions, hyperparameters, and a discussion of symmetry/equivariance limitations, including the important caveat that local reparameterization can break equivariance for irrep-based models.
weaknesses: The Bayesian formulation is not sound enough to support the central claims. The proposed prior depends on the learned mean weights theta, so it is not a fixed prior in the usual Bayesian sense. The resulting objective is closer to a regularized adaptive-noise training scheme than a principled posterior approximation, yet the paper repeatedly frames it as principled Bayesian inference.

There appear to be mathematical inconsistencies in the variational derivation. The KL expression in Appendix A seems to miss the standard 1/2 factor and differs from the KL between Gaussians with variances alpha theta^2 and p/(1-p) theta^2. The local reparameterization algorithm also appears to use alpha as a standard-deviation multiplier, whereas the main text defines alpha as controlling variance. These issues directly affect the claimed ELBO and training objective.

The method’s relationship to uncertainty is underjustified. The posterior is conditioned on each input structure through an inference network, which is not a conventional posterior over global model weights given the dataset. The paper does not clearly justify why this input-conditioned weight noise should provide calibrated epistemic uncertainty, especially under distribution shift.

The efficiency claims are overstated. The paper claims no inference overhead by setting the variational dropout coefficient to zero, but that only gives a deterministic MAP-style prediction and does not provide uncertainty. Uncertainty estimation still requires many stochastic forward passes, and the cost comparison to ensembles is therefore not presented fairly.

Experimental comparisons are not sufficiently rigorous. Several baseline results are taken from prior work while BLIP is newly tuned and rerun; ensemble entries sometimes have no variance despite the tables claiming averages over seeds; and some comparisons mix modern pretrained ORB models with older PaiNN results, making it hard to isolate the contribution of BLIP.

The active learning experiment is weakly controlled. It compares BLIP uncertainty selection mainly against BLIP random selection and a deterministic fine-tuning baseline, but lacks strong uncertainty-selection baselines such as ensembles, MC dropout, conformal methods, or alternative acquisition functions under matched compute.

Some evaluation definitions are unclear or possibly incorrect. In the MATPES appendix, the stated formula for energy uncertainty uses true and predicted energies rather than variance across stochastic predictions, which would be unavailable during acquisition. If this is a typo, it still undermines reproducibility; if not, it invalidates the active-learning uncertainty metric.

The paper lacks a sufficiently explicit limitations section. It notes important constraints, such as incompatibility of local reparameterization with some equivariant irrep-based MLIPs, but does not fully discuss how much this limits the advertised architecture-agnostic claim or how practitioners should choose between weight sampling and local reparameterization.

Reproducibility is only partial. Public datasets and many hyperparameters are provided, but I did not find a code release, exact preprocessing/split artifacts for all experiments, or enough detail to reproduce the ORB/MATPES active-learning pipeline and baseline tuning reliably.

Presentation is generally understandable but contains recurring imprecision and overclaiming. Claims such as architecture-agnostic, principled Bayesian, well-calibrated, and same inference-time efficiency are broader than the method and experiments justify. There are also typos and wording issues such as data-scarse, Coloumbs, memebers, and deepensembling.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: uncertainty quantification for ML interatomic potentials in low-data, OOD, and pretrained fine-tuning settings, where deep ensembles are often expensive.

BLIP is practically appealing: it is architecture-oriented, lightweight in parameter count, and can be used both from scratch and for fine-tuning pretrained MLIPs. The experiments cover several relevant regimes, including N-body dynamics, ammonia OOD generalization, silica glass, and MATPES active learning.

Empirical results are promising. BLIP improves or matches strong baselines on several predictive and UQ metrics: e.g. best GNN N-body MSE/NLL/CRPS, best ammonia force MAE and ECE, improved fine-tuned ORB performance on silica, and improved MATPES active-learning performance over random selection and non-BLIP fine-tuning.

The paper includes useful implementation details, dataset descriptions, hyperparameters, pseudocode, and a computational cost discussion. The discussion of equivariance and the limitation of local reparameterization for irrep-based models is thoughtful and relevant.
The contribution is significant for scientific ML practice because a single-model UQ method that works with pretrained potentials would be valuable if the empirical behavior is robust.
weaknesses: The Bayesian interpretation is not fully convincing. The variational posterior is input-dependent over weights, while a standard Bayesian neural network posterior is global given the dataset; the prior variance also depends on the learned weights. This makes the repeated claim of a principled Bayesian posterior stronger than what the formulation justifies.

There are technical ambiguities in the variational objective. The KL derivation appears to omit the usual 1/2 factor for Gaussian KL, and the use of a prior parameterized by theta makes the ELBO interpretation unclear. These may not invalidate the method empirically, but they weaken the soundness of the central theoretical framing.

Some comparisons are not fully satisfying. Several ammonia baselines are taken from Tan et al. rather than rerun under the same seed/reporting protocol; N-body deep ensemble uncertainty is reported with NA standard deviations despite other methods being averaged over seeds; silica results are mostly in a plot without complete numeric tables; and MATPES active learning lacks a comparison to ensemble-based acquisition.

The computational-cost claim needs more nuance. Mean prediction with zero perturbation has no overhead, but uncertainty quantification still requires multiple stochastic forward passes; the abstract and conclusions could more clearly distinguish predictive inference from UQ sampling cost.

Reproducibility is only partial. Datasets and many hyperparameters are described, but I did not see a code release, exact random seeds for all experiments, full numeric tables for all plotted results, or enough detail to reproduce the MATPES active-learning pool/split protocol unambiguously.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The paper acknowledges that local reparameterization does not directly support irrep-based equivariant models such as MACE/UMA, but broader limitations around calibration under distribution shift, DFT data bias, active-learning deployment, and failure modes in molecular simulation are underdeveloped.

Presentation is generally clear but has recurring typos and notation issues, including 'data-scarse', 'Coloumbs', inconsistent variance/std notation, and an apparently erroneous MATPES uncertainty equation that uses prediction errors rather than stochastic predictive variance.
